clue.text: Ali's question about our planet appears in Dawkins work

parts.note: the boxer Muhammad Ali famously called himself 'the greatest'
the possessive ending supplies its letter

explanation.surface: The boxer Ali's musing about the planet turns up in a book by the evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s of 'Ali's' is a letter of the answer, not a possessive: it begins SHOW.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Dawkins published a 2009 book on the evidence for evolution under this title, borrowed from the circus slogan.

clue.text: Take one groom's assistant with very high temperature to see clan member

parts.note: T for temperature, placed at the very top of this down answer
R is the recipe abbreviation, from Latin recipe, 'take'
the best man assists the bridegroom at a wedding

explanation.surface: A drinker with a fever is taken to see a member of the clan.
explanation.walkthrough: TRIBESMAN uses the letters of R, I and BEST MAN with the T of temperature lifted out of BEST MAN and moved to the very top of the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A tribesman belongs to a tribe, and a clan is another word for such a kinship group.

clue.text: A break when cardinals regularly feast?

parts.note: cardinal numbers, such as eleven, in the plural

indicators.note: regularly means taking letters at even intervals, every other one of the next word

parts.note: second and fourth letters of the word

explanation.surface: Seems to ask when the Church's cardinals pause to dine together.
explanation.walkthrough: Cardinals look like churchmen but are cardinal numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: Elevenses is a British term for a mid-morning snack or tea break, taken around eleven o'clock.

clue.text: Armature of motor that's unchanged after turning

indicators.note: a word that stays the same when read backwards is a palindrome

parts.note: the rotating part of an electric motor

explanation.surface: A note on a motor's moving part staying the same as it spins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning' suits the spinning part of the motor, but here it means reading the word backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The rotor is the rotating armature inside a motor or generator.

clue.text: Empty terminals around diametrically opposite points

indicators.note: around means one word encloses the other on both sides

parts.note: to tip is to empty out a container

explanation.surface: Deserted airport terminals somehow linked to points on opposite sides of the globe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Empty' reads as an adjective for the terminals but is the verb TIP.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipodes are places on exactly opposite sides of the Earth, as Britain and New Zealand roughly are.

clue.text: Old key found in lift

parts.note: the Alt key on a computer keyboard

explanation.surface: An antique key turns up in an elevator.
explanation.definitionFit: To exalt is to raise up or elevate, so it is a synonym of lift as a verb.

clue.text: Skybound risk taker I see during match point

indicators.note: during means occurring within, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: I plus LO, an old word for 'see!'

explanation.surface: A daredevil spotted at a tense moment in a tennis match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Match point' looks like one tennis phrase but splits into two pieces. A test match is an international cricket game.
explanation.definitionFit: A test pilot flies new aircraft to see whether they are safe, a hazardous job in the air.

clue.text: Father occasionally gets pissed as a newt

indicators.note: drunk letters stagger out of their proper order
occasionally means only now and then, so just every other letter is kept

explanation.surface: Dad now and then gets as drunk as a newt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed as a newt' is a British idiom for very drunk, so 'newt' hides as part of the cliché.
explanation.definitionFit: An eft is an old or dialect word for a newt, especially a young one.

clue.text: Expatriate chucked up life-prolonging concoction (English not Irish)

indicators.note: in a down clue, thrown upwards means the letters run bottom to top
X not Y means put one thing in place of the other

parts.note: an elixir of life was meant to prolong life

explanation.surface: An emigrant vomited up a potion meant to make life last longer.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the IR at the end of ELIXIR for E, then turn the whole word upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: An exile is someone living outside their homeland, as an expatriate does.

clue.text: Some young people finally drown in river

indicators.note: in places that letter inside the next piece

parts.note: the Tees, a river in north-east England

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A grim note on youngsters who ended up drowning in a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Teens is a collective term for teenagers, people aged thirteen to nineteen.

clue.text: Sluggish emperor is snubbed in Congress

indicators.note: in puts the shortened word inside the next piece

parts.note: IT is slang for sex, and congress can mean sexual intercourse

indicators.note: snubbed suggests cut short, like a snub nose, so the end is lopped off

explanation.surface: A lazy emperor is cold-shouldered by the US legislature.
explanation.walkthrough: Congress looks like the American parliament; here it is the old sense of sexual union.
explanation.definitionFit: Inert means inactive or slow to move, a synonym of sluggish.

clue.text: A sprinter resolved to come out

indicators.note: something resolved has been worked out and put into a new form

explanation.surface: A runner made up their mind to come out, perhaps publicly.
explanation.definitionFit: To transpire is to become known or emerge as fact, which is what coming out means here.

clue.text: When lecturing, I leave something to help the pupils

indicators.note: a lecturer speaks, so the word is taken as heard, not as written

parts.note: the pronoun spoken sounds like the organ of sight
to drop is to leave someone off, or leave out

explanation.surface: A teacher lecturing leaves something behind to help the students.
explanation.walkthrough: Pupils pretend to be schoolchildren but are the openings of the eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye-drop is a drop of medication put in the eye, so it helps the pupil in the anatomical sense.

clue.text: Half-exposed tenor at work? Not so

parts.note: OP is short for operation, so in op means working
less means to a smaller degree, not as much

explanation.surface: A singer half-undressed while working? Actually not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-exposed' means bare above the waist, not halfway visible.
explanation.definitionFit: Topless describes someone bare from the waist up, so half of the body is uncovered.

clue.text: For instance, newspapers, radio and TV service — main sources of information apparently

definitions.text: For instance, newspapers, radio and TV

parts.note: a Mass is a church service
media, plural of medium, the channels through which information reaches us

explanation.surface: Lists the main ways the public gets its news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apparently' flags that the second half is a loose description: the media are the chief channels of information.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspapers, radio and television are examples of the means of communication reaching large populations.

clue.text: Island with apples for voracious women

parts.note: eating apples are called eaters, as against cookers

explanation.surface: An island full of apples for greedy women.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain an eater is an apple for eating raw, a cooker one for cooking.
explanation.definitionFit: Maneaters are predatory women who use men up, voracious in a romantic sense.

clue.text: Half-cut Lord Admiral shot American native

indicators.note: half cut away means half of the first word is lost
shot means ruined or wrecked, so the letters are broken up

explanation.surface: A drunk naval commander shot a creature of the Americas.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-cut is British slang for drunk, but here it halves the word Lord.
explanation.definitionFit: The armadillo is an armoured mammal native to the Americas.

clue.text: Discover nonsense writer's first bit of nonsense

parts.note: Edward Lear wrote nonsense verse such as The Owl and the Pussy-cat

indicators.note: the first bit means only the opening letter is used

explanation.surface: Find out the start of a nonsense poet's absurdity.
explanation.definitionFit: To learn something can mean to find it out, a synonym of discover.

clue.text: Strange rationale for one causing estrangement

indicators.note: strange suggests something odd and out of its usual shape

explanation.surface: An odd justification for someone who drives people apart.
explanation.definitionFit: To alienate is to estrange, so an alienator is a person who brings about estrangement.

clue.text: Symphonic metal band's dark desire

explanation.surface: Names a heavy metal group's sinister longing.
explanation.walkthrough: Nightwish is a Finnish symphonic metal band.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the Finnish band famous for blending heavy metal with orchestral music.

clue.text: Bread is being imported this month

indicators.note: imported means brought inside, so one piece goes into another

explanation.surface: Bread is being shipped in from abroad this month.
explanation.walkthrough: Nisan is a month of the Hebrew calendar, around March to April.
explanation.definitionFit: Nisan is the first month of the Jewish religious year, when Passover falls.

clue.text: Maybe lied about drug, one featured in Beatles number

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the next pieces sit inside

parts.note: a lied is a German art song, so an example of a song

explanation.surface: Perhaps someone fibbed about a drug that featured in a Beatles song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lied' reads as the past tense of lie but is the German word for a song.
explanation.definitionFit: Something is a 1969 Beatles song written by George Harrison.

clue.text: Aid for driving glitzy dandy about

indicators.note: about means going around, so the second piece wraps the first

explanation.surface: A flashy dandy driving around offers help.
explanation.definitionFit: A fog lamp is a bright vehicle light that helps a driver see in mist.

clue.text: Knock down a storey

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to knock someone to the ground
second meaning: one level of a building

explanation.walkthrough: Knock down sounds like demolishing a building's storey, but the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Floor is a verb for felling someone with a punch and a noun for one level of a building.

clue.text: Georgia and Edward under curfew

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state
Ted is a short form of Edward

explanation.surface: Two people, Georgia and Edward, have been grounded.
explanation.walkthrough: Gated is British school and university slang for confined to college or home, especially at night.
explanation.definitionFit: A gated student is confined to the premises after hours, which is to be under curfew.

clue.text: Quiet chanteuse not loud? Certainly not

indicators.note: not means leave out, here the letter for loud

parts.note: f, forte, means loud in music

explanation.surface: A quiet singer who is not loud? Certainly not.
explanation.walkthrough: Piano is the musical marking for quiet, the opposite of forte.
explanation.definitionFit: In music piano is the direction to play softly, so it means quiet.

clue.text: Super network computer in Utah is no longer working

indicators.note: in places one piece within the next

parts.note: UT is the postal abbreviation for Utah
NC is the abbreviation for network computer

explanation.surface: A supercomputer in Utah has broken down.
explanation.definitionFit: Defunct means dead or out of operation, as a broken machine is.

clue.text: Half-hearted fellas at work? Not so

indicators.note: working letters are moved around into a new arrangement
half of the heart is removed, so one of the two central letters goes

explanation.surface: Are the blokes at work only half-hearted? Not so.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle of FELLAS is LL; losing half of it leaves FELAS.
explanation.definitionFit: False means untrue, so it amounts to saying a statement is not so.

clue.text: Working with ancient Greek, endless learners must be alert

indicators.note: endless means without its final letter

parts.note: on as in switched on, operating
L is learner, as on a British L-plate, so two of them

explanation.surface: Students working with ancient Greek texts need to stay sharp.
explanation.walkthrough: A Theban was a citizen of Thebes, a leading city of ancient Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: On the ball is an idiom for quick-witted and attentive, which is to be alert.

clue.text: Long stick used in mudflat hiking

indicators.note: used in says the answer is found inside the phrase that follows

parts.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A walker takes a long stick across the mudflats.
explanation.walkthrough: A lathi is the heavy bamboo staff carried by police in India.
explanation.definitionFit: A lathi is a long, often iron-bound stick used in South Asia as a weapon.

clue.text: Veiled woman stripped off to be free

indicators.note: stripped means the outer layer, its first and last letters, is taken off

parts.note: a bride traditionally wears a veil

explanation.surface: A woman throws off her veil to be free.
explanation.definitionFit: To be rid of something is to be free of it, so rid stands for free.

clue.text: See 1
